original_excerpt: The houses are scattered over the mohal in 13 hamlets. Except Maingal hamlet which has 7 houses closely built, other hamlets consist of one or two houses only. Maingal inhabited by Brahmins is surrounded by Gujjar hamlets on three sides... Gujjars do not have separate cattle sheds. Their kothas are divided internally.
neutral_summary: Settlement pattern reflects occupational cleavage: nuclear Brahmin cluster at Maingal surrounded by dispersed Gujjar forest hamlets inhabiting combined dwelling-byre kothas.
term_notes: Kotha is flat-roofed rough stone and timber pastoral dwelling.
coder_notes: Captures spatial manifestation of occupational and religious differentiation.

page_section: p. 33, Economy (Lohar Ironwork and Khalian Remuneration)
original_excerpt: The Lohar households repair the iron agricultural implements for cultivators. They do not charge cash fees but receive customary shares of unhusked grain (khalian) directly from the threshing floors at each harvest.
neutral_summary: Village blacksmiths maintain agricultural iron tools under customary jajmani barter, compensated in grain shares at harvest rather than cash.
term_notes: Khalian is customary harvest grain perquisites given at the threshing floor (khala).
coder_notes: Crucial evidence proving traditional customary service barter operating alongside cash economy.

page_section: p. 33, Economy (Gujjar Buffalo Dairying and Ghee Trade)
original_excerpt: All Gujjar households possess buffaloes. Castewise livestock statistics show that in 25 Gujjar households the number of buffaloes is 217... They sell milk locally and convert surplus into clarified butter (ghee) which is carried down to the Chamba town bazaar for sale.
neutral_summary: Muslim Gujjars specialize in commercial buffalo dairying, marketing surplus milk and clarified butter (ghee) in urban Chamba markets.
term_notes: Ghee represents the primary commodified pastoral output linking remote hamlets to urban markets.
coder_notes: Demonstrates market integration of pastoral household economy.

original_excerpt: Muslim Gujjars are the converts from Hindus. But now they have become devout Muslims and practise Islamic customs. It is due to passage of time that they have slowly imbibed the Islamic way of life, yet live in peace with Hindu neighbours.
neutral_summary: Muslim Gujjars maintain distinct Islamic religious identity while maintaining peaceful, interdependent neighbourly relations with orthodox Hindu Brahmins.
term_notes: Highlights peaceful multi-religious co-existence grounded in mutual economic utility.
coder_notes: Directly addresses the religious relations facet of the core research question.
